channel.title: Chrome Web Platform Ecosystem Updates
channel.description: Weekly web intelligence on ChromeStatus features, web standards, and developer community pulse

item.title: HTML-in-canvas — Chrome 157 Ecosystem Update
item.description:
HTML-in-canvas (Chrome 157, Enabled by default)

HTML-in-canvas enables customizing the rendering of html using canvas with new primitives to manage canvas layout, drawing capabilities, rendering events for DOM-to-canvas synchronization, and geometry update capabilities for canvas-to-DOM synchronization.

Ecosystem Analysis: The HTML-in-canvas feature (shipping in Chrome 157) bridges a long-standing gap by allowing native HTML/CSS rendering, accessibility, and interactivity inside high-performance WebGL/WebGPU canvases. While it solves major pain points for rich graphics applications and UI frameworks, it is still navigating early-stage multi-stakeholder design reviews across browser engines.

item.title: Local network access restrictions — Chrome 156 Ecosystem Update
item.description:
Local network access restrictions (Chrome 156, Stepped rollout)

Chrome 142 restricted the ability to make requests to the user's local network, gated behind a permission prompt. A local network request is any request from a public website to a local IP address or loopback, or from a local website (for example, intranet) to loopback. Gating the ability for websites to perform these requests behind a permission mitigates the risk of cross-site request forgery attacks against local network devices such as routers, and reduces the ability of sites to use these requests to fingerprint the user's local network. This permission is restricted to secure contexts. If granted, the permissions additionally relax mixed content blocking for local network requests (since many local devices are not able to obtain publicly trusted TLS certificates for various reasons). This work supersedes a prior effort called [Private Network Access](https://chromestatus.com/feature/5737414355058688), which used preflight requests to have local devices opt in. For more information on this feature, see [Adapting your website for new Local Network Access restrictions in Chrome](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1QQkqehw8umtAgz5z0um7THx-aoU251p705FbIQjDuGs/edit?usp=sharing). Chrome 145 introduced more granular permissions for websites requesting access to a user's local network. The previous single `local-network-access permission` is being split into two distinct permissions: * `local-network`: Grants access to IP addresses in the local network space (for example, intranets, internal devices). * `loopback-network`: Grants access to loopback IP addresses (for example, `localhost`, `127.0.0.1`). The old `local-network` permission will remain as an alias, ensuring existing configurations and permissions policies continue to function as expected. This change provides both users and Admins with more precise control over how websites interact with internal network resources. Current enterprise policies managing local network access will not be affected by this change. Chrome 146 introduces two new enterprise policies for managing local network access restrictions: [LocalNetworkAccessIpAddressSpaceOverrides](https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#LocalNetworkAccessIpAddressSpaceOverrides) and [LocalNetworkAccessPermissionsPolicyDefaultEnabled](https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#LocalNetworkAccessPermissionsPolicyDefaultEnabled). These policies can be set using [custom configurations](https://support.google.com/chrome/a/answer/14749672). Chrome 147 expands Local Network Access restrictions to include WebSocket and WebTransport connections. In Chrome 156, the [LocalNetworkAccessRestrictionsTemporaryOptOut](https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#LocalNetworkAccessRestrictionsTemporaryOptOut) policy will be removed.

Ecosystem Analysis: Chrome has moved forward with Local Network Access restrictions, shifting away from the complex Private Network Access preflight model to an explicit browser permission prompt split into local-network and loopback-network controls. While this hardens security against cross-site request forgery and local network fingerprinting, it introduces severe friction for web apps that interface with local hardware, developer tooling, and intranet servers. The feature currently sits in limited availability, heavily driven by Chromium with other engine stances still materializing.

item.title: Support for WebHID — Chrome 154 Ecosystem Update
item.description:
Support for WebHID (Chrome 154, In developer trial (Behind a flag))

WebHID allows web applications to interact with a wider range of devices. Standard examples of Human Interface Devices (HIDs) include mice, keyboards, touchscreens, and gamepads. Those are accessible with high-level input events. However, specialized HIDs and HID features (for example, custom keyboards, game controllers, and call control headsets) require extended access. WebHID allows web applications to request access, send and receive HID reports, and retrieve information about the report descriptor. This feature was previously launched on desktop platforms (Windows, macOS, Linux, and ChromeOS). Support on Android is planned for Chrome 157. To read more, see [Connect to uncommon HID devices](https://developer.chrome.com/docs/extensions/how-to/web-platform/webhid). This feature can be controlled by the following enterprise policies: * [DefaultWebHidGuardSetting](https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#DefaultWebHidGuardSetting) * [WebHidAllowAllDevicesForUrls](https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#WebHidAllowAllDevicesForUrls) * [WebHidAllowDevicesForUrls](https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#WebHidAllowDevicesForUrls) * [WebHidAllowDevicesWithHidUsagesForUrls](https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#WebHidAllowDevicesWithHidUsagesForUrls) * [WebHidAskForUrls](https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#WebHidAskForUrls) * [WebHidBlockedForUrls](https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#WebHidBlockedForUrls)

Ecosystem Analysis: The WebHID API allows web applications to communicate directly with specialized Human Interface Devices, expanding from its initial desktop launch to support extension service workers, dedicated workers, and upcoming Android integration. Despite its utility for hardware-interactive web applications and companion tools, it remains a Chromium-specific feature with limited cross-browser consensus. Mozilla holds a negative standards position due to security and fingerprinting considerations.

item.title: Deprecate and remove: Attribution Reporting API — Chrome 153 Ecosystem Update
item.description:
Deprecate and remove: Attribution Reporting API (Chrome 153, Deprecated)

The Attribution Reporting API is a privacy-preserving web API designed to measure ad conversions without third-party cookies or user tracking across sites. Following Chrome's announcement that the current approach to third-party cookies will be maintained, we are now planning to deprecate and remove the Attribution Reporting API (along with other Privacy Sandbox APIs). [0]: https://privacysandbox.com/news/privacy-sandbox-next-steps/

Ecosystem Analysis: Following Google's decision to maintain third-party cookies rather than phase them out, the Attribution Reporting API is being deprecated and removed in Chrome 153. Due to low industry adoption and a lack of cross-browser support from Safari/WebKit and Firefox/Gecko, Google is scaling back these Privacy Sandbox components to refocus on alternative interoperable standards.

item.title: CSS scroll-marker-group modes — Chrome 154 Ecosystem Update
item.description:
CSS scroll-marker-group modes (Chrome 154, Enabled by default)

The scroll-marker-group property is enhaced to support modes: 1) 'links' - The generated ::scroll-marker-group operates in "links" mode, functioning like a navigation list. This is the default mode if omitted. 2) 'tabs' - The generated ::scroll-marker-group operates in "tabs" mode, functioning like a tablist. Each mode changes focus order and accessibility behavior of ::scroll-marker-group and ::scroll-markers, following WAI-ARIA patterns. More details: # The links mode (default) This mode is designed to mimic standard Navigation Landmarks combined with fragment anchors. ## Semantic roles The ::scroll-marker-group takes on the navigation role, and the ::scroll-marker elements take on the link role. This perfectly maps to the <nav> + <a> structural pattern. ## Keyboard navigation All ::scroll-marker elements are sequential tab stops, natively acting like a list of standard anchor links. ## Unaffected targets The originating elements do not get forced into any role, leaving the document's natural semantic structure intact. ## Activation focus management When a link marker is activated, it sets the sequential focus navigation starting point to the target element (the originating element), and focus is lost from the marker. This mimics the native behavior of clicking a standard internal <a href="#target"> link. # The tabs mode This mode is designed to natively replicate the Tabs Pattern and serves as the interactive foundation for the Tabbed Carousel Pattern. ## Semantic roles The ::scroll-marker-group is implicitly assigned the tablist role, ::scroll-marker elements act as tab roles, and their originating elements get the tabpanel role. This mirrors the required WAI-ARIA Tabs structure. ## Keyboard navigation (roving tabindex) It follows the complex keyboard interactions outlined in standard practices. Only the active ::scroll-marker acts as a tab stop. Users use arrow keys to navigate the focusgroup (switching between markers), preventing the "tab trap" of having to tab through 20 carousel dots. ## Focus scope management The marker acts as a focus navigation scope owner. Pressing Tab from the active marker moves focus directly into the active tabpanel content, matching the specification for tabbed interfaces. ## Tree pruning Content from inactive tabs is explicitly hidden from the accessibility tree. This mimics the expected behavior of aria-hidden="true" or inert on inactive tab panels, saving developers from manually scripting state changes. ## Activation focus When a marker is activated, focus is retained on the marker, which is exactly how standard tabs operate.

Ecosystem Analysis: The CSS scroll-marker-group modes feature introduces native 'links' and 'tabs' behaviors to scroll markers, dramatically improving semantic alignment and keyboard navigation for declarative carousels and tabs. While Chromium has advanced implementation to enabled-by-default status, the feature lacks cross-browser baseline status and faces substantial accessibility scrutiny from other vendors.

item.title: Language Detector API on Android — Chrome 157 Ecosystem Update
item.description:
Language Detector API on Android (Chrome 157, Enabled by default)

Exposes the LanguageDetector JavaScript Web API on Chrome for Android (Clank). This allows web applications to detect text languages locally on mobile devices using fast, privacy-preserving, and offline-capable on-device machine learning models and not rely on cloud endpoints.

Ecosystem Analysis: The Language Detector API rolling out in Chrome 157 for Android brings local, privacy-preserving, and offline-capable text language identification to mobile web apps via built-in AI models. However, the ecosystem remains heavily fragmented as the feature lacks cross-browser consensus, sitting at Limited Availability with a negative position from Mozilla and an open, cautious posture from WebKit.

item.title: Digital Credentials API (issuance support) — Chrome 155 Ecosystem Update
item.description:
Digital Credentials API (issuance support) (Chrome 155, Enabled by default)

This Web Platform feature enables issuing websites (e.g., a university, government agency, or bank) to securely initiate the provisioning (issuance) process of digital credentials directly into a user's mobile wallet application. On Android, this capability leverages the Android IdentityCredential CredMan system (Credential Manager). On Desktop, it leverages cross-device approaches using the CTAP protocol similar to Digital Credentials presentation.

Ecosystem Analysis: The Digital Credentials API (issuance support) extends browser-mediated identity handling to allow issuing bodies like universities and banks to provision credentials directly into user mobile wallets. Currently rolling out in Chrome (targeting Milestone 155), it relies heavily on native mobile infrastructure like Android's Credential Manager and OpenID4VCI protocols, though it lacks cross-browser interoperability and Baseline status.

item.title: Deprecate and Remove Protected Audience — Chrome 153 Ecosystem Update
item.description:
Deprecate and Remove Protected Audience (Chrome 153, Deprecated)

The Protected Audience API provides a method of interest-group advertising without third-party cookies or user tracking across sites. Following Chrome's announcement that the current approach to third-party cookies will be maintained, we are now planning to deprecate and remove the Protected Audience API (along with certain other Privacy Sandbox APIs, as outlined on the Privacy Sandbox feature status page).

Ecosystem Analysis: The Protected Audience API (formerly FLEDGE) is slated for deprecation and removal in Chrome 153 following Google's decision to maintain third-party cookies. With ecosystem interest having collapsed and usage metrics dropping significantly, the feature is being phased out alongside other targeted Privacy Sandbox advertising components.

item.title: JPEG XL decoding support (image/jxl) in blink — Chrome 155 Ecosystem Update
item.description:
JPEG XL decoding support (image/jxl) in blink (Chrome 155, Enabled by default)

Adds support for decoding JPEG XL (image/jxl) images in Blink using jxl-rs, a memory-safe pure Rust decoder (https://github.com/libjxl/jxl-rs). JPEG XL is a modern image format standardized as ISO/IEC 18181 that offers progressive decoding for improved perceived loading performance, support for wide color gamut, HDR, and high bit depth, and support for animation.

Ecosystem Analysis: JPEG XL (`image/jxl`) decoding support has officially achieved cross-browser availability, marked by Chrome 155 enabling the format by default in Blink using `jxl-rs`, a memory-safe pure Rust decoder developed by Google Research. Following Safari's baseline adoption in version 17 and Firefox enabling default support in version 158, all major browser engines now support native JXL decoding. The browser consensus has shifted from past C++ attack surface concerns to enthusiastic alignment around a shared, memory-safe Rust architecture.

item.title: CSS position-visibility:anchor{s}-valid — Chrome 157 Ecosystem Update
item.description:
CSS position-visibility:anchor{s}-valid (Chrome 157, Enabled by default)

The `anchors-valid` value was implemented as part of https://crbug.com/329703412 but subsequently reverted, due to spec questions about the exact definition of the value. Since that time, the value has been renamed to `anchor-valid` (see https://chromestatus.com/feature/5136123851571200) and also better defined to be clear that only the default anchor matters, resolving a lot of ambiguity, and making this value shippable.

Ecosystem Analysis: The `position-visibility: anchor-valid` property value (formerly `anchors-valid`) has been stabilized and implemented to automatically hide anchor-positioned elements like tooltips or dropdowns if their default anchor reference cannot be resolved. Following recent spec clarifications resolving ambiguities around multi-anchor definitions, the feature has been successfully shipped in modern browser milestones, driving improved alignment across the CSS Anchor Positioning ecosystem.

item.title: Long Animation Frames style and layout duration — Chrome 157 Ecosystem Update
item.description:
Long Animation Frames style and layout duration (Chrome 157, Enabled by default)

Add `styleDuration` and `forcedStyleDuration` information to the Long Animation Frame API, enabling developers to distinguish style and layout times.

Ecosystem Analysis: The Long Animation Frames (LoAF) API has been expanded to include granular sub-metrics like `styleDuration` and `forcedStyleDuration` (along with layout durations), offering unprecedented visibility into CSS performance bottlenecks. While fully enabled in Chromium-based browsers, it lacks baseline interoperability as other engines have yet to ship matching implementations.

item.title: Renewed HTML insertion&streaming methods — Chrome 157 Ecosystem Update
item.description:
Renewed HTML insertion&streaming methods (Chrome 157, Enabled by default)

Expose multiple HTML setting methods that provide a coherent story for dynamically inserting markup into an existing document. - Positional methods (before/after/append/prepend/replaceWith) that take HTML as argument, effectively replacing insertAdjacentHTML. - Streaming methods (stream{Append}HTML{Unsafe}) which return a WritableStream, receiving text as input and parsing HMHL. - Passing {runScripts} as part of SetHTMLUnsafeOptions, mimicking createContextualFragment behavior. - Supporting createParserOptions in trusted types, allowing trusted types to override scripting mode and sanitizer.

Ecosystem Analysis: The 'Renewed HTML insertion & streaming methods' feature unifies and modernizes dynamic markup injection and parsing into a coherent set of positional, streaming, and safe/unsafe variants. It is enabled by default in Chrome, addressing historical developer fragmentation issues related to disjointed APIs like insertAdjacentHTML.

item.title: Margin-trim — Chrome 155 Ecosystem Update
item.description:
Margin-trim (Chrome 155, Enabled by default)

The `margin-trim` CSS property may be used to omit margins before or after the first or last child of a container. This is supported on regular block containers and multicol containers. This is somewhat similar to the effect caused by the margin quirk that is applied to P, H1, H2... elements inside BODY and table cell elements (in quirks mode), but more powerful, generic, and expressive. Note: A previous version of the spec also applied this for flex and grid containers, but this has been removed.

Ecosystem Analysis: The margin-trim CSS property enables containers to cleanly discard adjoining child margins, eliminating classic container-edge spacing bugs and fragile structural selectors. Long pioneered exclusively by Safari since version 16.4, the specification underwent refinements to focus on block and multi-column containers, with Chromium shipping default enablement in Chrome 155. Cross-browser Baseline availability remains limited, but engine consensus is firmly positive across all major vendors.

item.title: Avoid caching module failures — Chrome 156 Ecosystem Update
item.description:
Avoid caching module failures (Chrome 156, Enabled by default)

Currently web developers cannot retry failed module loads, as these failures are being cached (and retries just result in immediate failures). This change to the module loading behavior enables failed module loads to be manually retried (e.g. by calling `import()` again), solving real developer (and user) pain when it comes to using modules over unstable networks.

Ecosystem Analysis: The 'Avoid caching module failures' update resolves a longstanding flaw in the HTML specification where transient network or HTTP fetch failures were permanently cached in the document's module map. With the merge of the specification update in the WHATWG HTML standard, all major browser engines have moved to align, eliminating sticky fetch errors and allowing dynamic imports to be retried. The platform consensus shifts module loading priorities from strict failure determinism toward real-world network resilience.

item.title: Optional browser optimization for Service Workers — Chrome 154 Ecosystem Update
item.description:
Optional browser optimization for Service Workers (Chrome 154, Stepped rollout)

Chrome 154 includes an optional browser optimization mode that changes existing service worker behavior. In ServiceWorkerAutoPreload mode, the browser issues the network request in parallel with the service worker bootstrap. If the `fetch` handler returns the response with `respondWith()`, the browser consumes the network request result inside the `fetch` handler. If the `fetch` handler result is fallback, it passes the network response directly to the browser. Admins can control this feature using an enterprise policy called [ServiceWorkerAutoPreloadEnabled](https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#ServiceWorkerAutoPreloadEnabled).

Ecosystem Analysis: ServiceWorkerAutoPreload has successfully merged into the W3C Service Worker specification and is rolling out across Chromium-based engines as a browser-level optimization to eradicate worker cold-start latency. By dispatching navigation requests concurrently during service worker bootstrap and reusing the in-flight response inside fetch handlers, the feature transparently solves a long-standing PWA performance bottleneck. Cross-vendor alignment is firmly established following Mozilla's formal endorsement and collaborative refinement during the specification process.

item.title: Single-axis scroll containers — Chrome 156 Ecosystem Update
item.description:
Single-axis scroll containers (Chrome 156, Enabled by default)

Extends the `overflow` property to support scrollable values together with `clip` (for example, `overflow: scroll clip`). This allows `position: sticky` to be constrained by different ancestor scroll containers per axis, and gives authors a way to ensure an axis using `overflow: clip` stays in place.

Ecosystem Analysis: Single-axis scroll containers resolve a decade-old CSS limitation by permitting scrollable overflow values to pair with `clip`, ending the automatic coercion of containers into two-dimensional scrollers. Chromium leads implementation by enabling the capability by default in Chrome 156 following extensive testing channels, resolving foundational pain points for simultaneous horizontal scrolling and vertical sticky positioning. While the W3C CSS Working Group formally resolved the specification change under Issue #865 and the W3C TAG closed review as satisfied, multi-engine interoperability is still pending stable rollouts across Gecko and WebKit.

item.title: CSS random() function — Chrome 156 Ecosystem Update
item.description:
CSS random() function (Chrome 156, Enabled by default)

The random() function brings generative randomness to CSS, allowing web authors to generate a random numeric value within a specified range. For example, web authors can use random() to scatter elements randomly within their container: .dot { /* Position each dot randomly */ position: absolute; top: random(0%, 100%); left: random(0%, 100%); } This feature also includes caching controls. By default, each random() function resolves to a new, distinct value. Web authors can override this default by passing a <random-key> value as the function's first argument to control how random values are shared across properties and elements.

Ecosystem Analysis: The CSS random() function brings generative numeric randomness natively into stylesheets, eliminating long-standing reliance on JavaScript hacks and precalculated variables for organic UI variation. Spearheaded by WebKit and enabled by default in Chrome 156, the feature has achieved unanimous vendor alignment across the CSS Working Group. While Safari and Chromium lead browser availability, ecosystem-wide Baseline interoperability awaits Gecko's pending implementation release.

item.title: Immersive Audio Model and Formats (IAMF) decoding support — Chrome 153 Ecosystem Update
item.description:
Immersive Audio Model and Formats (IAMF) decoding support (Chrome 153, Enabled by default)

Adds support for decoding and playing back the Immersive Audio Model and Formats (IAMF) container within HTML media elements via Media Source Extensions (MSE). IAMF is an open, royalty-free spatial audio format that supports channel-based, scene-based, and object-based audio presentations. Supporting this standard allows web developers to deliver consistent, immersive 3D audio experiences across different devices without relying on proprietary formats or managing complex discrete audio channel routing in JavaScript.

Ecosystem Analysis: IAMF (Immersive Audio Model and Formats) decoding support has landed natively in Chromium (Chrome 153) via Media Source Extensions, offering an open and royalty-free alternative to proprietary 3D audio formats like Dolby Atmos. While Google and hardware partners like Samsung are pushing adoption—commercializing it under names like Eclipsa Audio—cross-browser consensus is still in its infancy. Mozilla and WebKit engineers have recently opened standards-position evaluation threads, but neither Gecko nor Safari has committed to an implementation timeline yet.

item.title: Algorithm Updates in WebCrypto — Chrome 155 Ecosystem Update
item.description:
Algorithm Updates in WebCrypto (Chrome 155, Enabled by default)

Add post-quantum cryptography and a common symmetric AEAD to the set of cryptographic algorithms available in the Web Cryptography API. This will enable developers to have access browser-provided implementations of common quantum-resistant cryptographic algorithms standardized by NIST. * ML-KEM - 768, 1024 * ML-DSA - 44, 65, 87 * ChaCha20-Poly1305 * X-Wing

Ecosystem Analysis: Chromium's addition of NIST post-quantum primitives (ML-KEM, ML-DSA, X-Wing) and ChaCha20-Poly1305 in Chrome 155 brings native, side-channel-resistant cryptographic operations directly to the browser via the Web Cryptography API. While security engineers and cryptographic library maintainers welcome the ability to replace heavy WebAssembly or JavaScript implementations with BoringSSL-backed routines, formal consensus across browser engines remains divided. Because modern algorithms are not strictly mandatory to implement across all engines, the update currently acts as a forward-looking Chromium enhancement rather than an interoperable baseline.

item.title: Connection Allowlists - Embedded Enforcement — Chrome 157 Ecosystem Update
item.description:
Connection Allowlists - Embedded Enforcement (Chrome 157, Origin trial)

Connection Allowlists (https://chromestatus.com/feature/5175745573945344) is a feature designed to provide explicit control over external endpoints by restricting connections initiated via the Fetch API or other web platform APIs from a document or worker. This aspect of the feature extends Connection Allowlists to support embedded enforcement on iFrames and nested documents/workers. This allows the parent document to enforce restrictions on embedded content where they can choose to opt in or not load. More details on the proposal can be found here: https://github.com/WICG/connection-allowlists

Ecosystem Analysis: Connection Allowlists - Embedded Enforcement extends the emerging native browser 'egress firewall' to nested contexts, ensuring iframes and workers cannot circumvent parent network restrictions or act as data exfiltration vectors. Incubated within the WICG by Google and Microsoft Edge engineers, the core specification aims to replace the ergonomic pitfalls of CSP connect-src, with the embedded enforcement mechanism advancing into Chrome Origin Trials. While cross-browser engine consensus is generally favorable towards cleaner exfiltration primitives, production cross-engine availability remains in development.

item.title: CSS corner shorthand properties — Chrome 157 Ecosystem Update
item.description:
CSS corner shorthand properties (Chrome 157, Enabled by default)

Implements the CSS corner shorthand and per-corner sub-shorthands (corner-top-left, corner-top-right, corner-bottom-left, corner-bottom-right) as well as physical (corner-top, corner-bottom) and logical (corner-block-start, corner-block-end, etc.) edge shorthands. These allow setting both border-radius and corner-shape for individual corners in a single declaration. Additionally, corners is retained as a compat alias for the corner shorthand. sampler: https://static.januschka.com/i-425897047/ CL: https://chromium-review.googlesource.com/c/chromium/src/+/7747994

Ecosystem Analysis: The CSS corner shorthand feature streamlines modern UI layout design by combining border-radius and corner-shape values into a single property declaration per corner, edge, or logical block. Landing natively in Chromium-based browsers, it addresses a long-standing developer pain point by eliminating the need for separate properties or external hacks like clip-path and SVGs. While Chrome implements the spec directly, overall cross-browser web platform tests and adoption remain in early experimental states.

item.title: WebAudio: Configurable render quantum — Chrome 153 Ecosystem Update
item.description:
WebAudio: Configurable render quantum (Chrome 153, Enabled by default)

Adds an optional renderSizeHint to AudioContext and OfflineAudioContext. This allows developers to customize the WebAudio render quantum size by passing a specific integer, use the default of 128 frames by omitting the hint or passing "default", or request that the User-Agent select an optimal size by specifying "hardware".

Ecosystem Analysis: Configurable render quantum in WebAudio introduces the `renderSizeHint` option to AudioContext and OfflineAudioContext, allowing engines to diverge from the historically rigid 128-sample-frame processing block. Standardized as part of the Web Audio API 1.1 specification and enabled by default in Chromium, it addresses a longstanding architectural bottleneck for browser-based digital audio workstations (DAWs), DSP libraries, and low-latency communication tools. While developer interest is high and specification roots stem directly from working group consensus, formal multi-engine implementation remains uneven across Safari and Firefox.

item.title: js-profiling in dedicated workers — Chrome 154 Ecosystem Update
item.description:
js-profiling in dedicated workers (Chrome 154, In developer trial (Behind a flag))

Allows js-profiling in dedicated workers This feature enables the JavaScript Self‑Profiling (js-profiling) API in Dedicated Workers, while remaining gated by Document Policy. It allows developers to obtain low‑overhead CPU attribution for JavaScript execution in workers, with Document Policy support for workers tracked separately.

Ecosystem Analysis: The 'js-profiling in dedicated workers' feature extends the JavaScript Self-Profiling API to background worker threads, addressing a critical visibility gap for offloaded performance-critical tasks. While currently progressing in Chromium (behind a developer trial flag), it remains constrained by cross-browser interoperability challenges due to its complex dependency on Document Policy semantics in workers.

item.title: Use scroll-snap-type: pair to snap to a single element — Chrome 156 Ecosystem Update
item.description:
Use scroll-snap-type: pair to snap to a single element (Chrome 156, Enabled by default)

https://github.com/w3c/csswg-drafts/issues/9519 Add a "pair" keyword to scroll-snap-type. If used, when the container scroll snaps to an element on one axis, it should snap to the same element on the other axis. In the existing spec, the "both" keyword allows the scroll container to select snap targets in X and Y axes independently and snap to different targets.

Ecosystem Analysis: The `scroll-snap-type: pair` keyword resolves a longstanding CSS Scroll Snap limitation where `both` evaluates horizontal and vertical axes independently, potentially snapping to two disparate targets. By treating multi-axis snap targets as unified 2D coordinates, `pair` guarantees the scroller locks onto the same element across both dimensions. Chromium is shipping the feature enabled by default in Chrome 156 with upstreamed Web Platform Tests, while broad multi-engine consensus is forming.

item.title: Deprecate and Remove: document.requestStorageAccessFor — Chrome 153 Ecosystem Update
item.description:
Deprecate and Remove: document.requestStorageAccessFor (Chrome 153, Deprecated)

The requestStorageAccessFor (rSAFor) API is an extension to the Storage Access API that allows a top-level site to request access to unpartitioned ("first-party") cookies on behalf of embedded sites. Browsers will have discretion to grant or deny access, with mechanisms like Related Website Sets (RWS) membership as a potential signal. This allows for use of the Storage Access API by top-level sites. Following Chrome's announcement that the current approach to third-party cookies will be maintained, we are now planning to deprecate and remove rSAFor, as it is only usable in Chrome to request storage access between RWS sites. Related Website Sets will also be deprecated via a separate intent.

Ecosystem Analysis: The `document.requestStorageAccessFor()` (rSAFor) API is being deprecated and removed in Chrome (targeting milestones such as Chrome 153), following Chrome's shift in its third-party cookie strategy. Because the API was largely tied to Chrome's Related Website Sets (RWS) ecosystem and lacked multi-browser standardization interest, its removal trims proprietary tech debt. Developers relying on it must audit their codebases and transition away from top-level storage access requests.

item.title: Pause media playback on not-visible iframes — Chrome 155 Ecosystem Update
item.description:
Pause media playback on not-visible iframes (Chrome 155, Enabled by default)

Adds a "media-playback-while-not-visible" permission policy to allow embedders to pause audible media playback of embedded iframes which are currently hidden - i.e. "display" property set to "none"; "visibility" property set to "hidden"; or zero-area (width or height equal to 0). While hidden, attempts made by the embedded iframe to render audible media will be blocked. When the frame is shown again the prohibitions should be lifted. This should allow developers to build more user-friendly experiences and to also improve the performance by letting the browser handle the playback of content that is not visible to users.

Ecosystem Analysis: The "Pause media playback on not-visible iframes" feature introduces the `media-playback-while-not-visible` Permission Policy, allowing embedders to halt audible media in hidden iframes without completely destroying the frame context. It addresses long-standing UX and performance issues associated with background audio in collapsed widgets or tabs. Browser vendor consensus is shaping up positively, with Mozilla Gecko expressing support due to parallel power-efficiency goals.

item.title: scroll-axis-lock — Chrome 153 Ecosystem Update
item.description:
scroll-axis-lock (Chrome 153, Enabled by default)

scroll-axis-lock is a CSS property that authors can use to instruct browsers not to constrain a user's scrolling gesture to one axis. Web browsers often "lock" a user's scrolling gesture to a single axis when that gesture starts with significantly more movement in one axis than in the perpendicular axis. In many cases, this behavior improves the user's experience by avoiding accidental scrolls along the perpendicular axis when the user's intent was to scroll only one axis. However, in cases where an author wishes their element to always be diagonally scrollable, this locking behavior forces the user to start their gesture at an angle that doesn't trigger the locking, often not in alignment with the author's intended user experience.

Ecosystem Analysis: The CSS scroll-axis-lock property introduced in CSS Overflow 5 has shipped enabled by default in Chrome 153, offering developers a native declarative mechanism to disable directional axis-locking for two-dimensional scroll containers. Consensus across standard bodies is strong, highlighted by a satisfied W3C TAG review and positive reception in both Mozilla and WebKit standards discussions. The ecosystem views it as a significant ergonomic win that eliminates the need for heavy JavaScript touch-interception workarounds in maps, design canvases, and multi-directional carousels.

item.title: Ship anchor-visible and anchor-valid, and deprecate the plural versions — Chrome 157 Ecosystem Update
item.description:
Ship anchor-visible and anchor-valid, and deprecate the plural versions (Chrome 157, Enabled by default)

The CSSWG resolved to rename `anchors-valid` --> `anchor-valid` [1] and `anchors-visible` --> `anchor-visible` [2]. To accomplish this, we'll rename the properties to the singular variants, and add aliases from the plural versions to the singular versions. At a later date, we will remove the plural variants. This chromestatus is only about shipping the new versions, and deprecating the old ones (but not removing them). [1] https://github.com/w3c/csswg-drafts/issues/10201#issuecomment-4180411971 [2] https://github.com/w3c/csswg-drafts/issues/10201#issuecomment-4390233490

Ecosystem Analysis: Chrome 157 ships the rename of CSS anchor positioning properties from `anchors-valid` and `anchors-visible` to their singular forms, `anchor-valid` and `anchor-visible`, aligning with CSSWG resolutions. While backward-compatible aliases are temporarily maintained, developers need to transition to the singular syntax to stay aligned with the evolving spec and maintain future-proof codebases.

item.title: Expose CSSStyleValue hierarchy to Worker contexts — Chrome 154 Ecosystem Update
item.description:
Expose CSSStyleValue hierarchy to Worker contexts (Chrome 154, Enabled by default)

The CSS Typed OM spec exposes the CSSStyleValue hierarchy to worker global scopes ([Exposed=(Window, Worker, PaintWorklet, LayoutWorklet)]), but Blink only exposed CSSStyleValue, CSSKeywordValue, CSSNumericValue, CSSUnitValue and CSSUnparsedValue to Window and the worklets. As a result these constructors were undefined in Workers, unlike in Firefox and Safari.

Ecosystem Analysis: With Chromium exposing the CSSStyleValue hierarchy to Worker global scopes in Chrome 154 release notes, Blink resolves a longstanding omission where Typed OM constructors were exposed to Window and Worklets but missing in standard Web Workers. This change aligns Chromium with the W3C CSS Typed OM specification and enables off-main-thread CSS object creation and numeric arithmetic. Cross-engine consensus is unified, resolving a cross-thread inconsistency that previously hindered background style computation.

item.title: Remove FencedFrame element and window.fence APIs — Chrome 156 Ecosystem Update
item.description:
Remove FencedFrame element and window.fence APIs (Chrome 156, Deprecated)

Fenced frames are nested frames that embed content onto a page without the ability to share data between the fenced frame and its embedder. window.fence APIs include Fenced frames Ads reporting (FFAR) JS APIs that were created for privacy-safe ads reporting from FFs created using Protected Audience and SelectURL and getNestedConfigs() to support PA component ads. This intent is for removing both of these. Fenced frames element removal will be two step as detailed below. With the removal (or stub API replacement) of PA and selectURL, FFs can no longer be navigated and thus it is safe to remove them. Fenced frames are only able to be navigated using the urn:uuid in a FencedFrameConfig[1], which can only be created using the return values from runAdAuction and selectURL. These APIs are being deprecated and removed in M152 as per the following Intent threads: Protected Audience[2], Shared Storage[3]. Plan: Given that the fenced frames element can no longer be navigated, we propose removing the element from the code in the following phases: 1. M156: Keep the fenced frame element and its associated IDL dependencies as stubs. This is to ensure no JS call throws, e.g.calling fenced-frame-element.config.setSharedStorageContext(). 2. M156: In the same milestone we will also stub the window.fence APIs completely. Since there is no FF document navigation, these APIs cannot be invoked anymore, so it will be a no-op. 3. M157 Canary/Beta: Begin a controlled rollout of the stub FF HTML element removal via a field trial. Note that removing the element will resolve it to HTMLUnknownElement. At this point we are requesting approvals for all of the above steps. 4. M157 Stable: Assuming there are no regressions or breakage after reaching 1% stable, we will request additional approval for full removal of the FF element. [1]https://source.chromium.org/chromium/chromium/src/+/main:third_party/blink/renderer/core/html/fenced_frame/fenced_frame_config.idl [2]https://groups.google.com/a/chromium.org/g/blink-dev/c/k_nubsMb97g/m/awPD4IGLBAAJ [3]https://groups.google.com/a/chromium.org/g/blink-dev/c/uh5Ke6qyegc/m/WFTFnhyJBAAJ

Ecosystem Analysis: Following Chrome's strategic pivot regarding third-party cookies and Privacy Sandbox ad auction mechanics, the `<fencedframe>` element and `window.fence` APIs are being stubbed in Chrome 156 and systematically removed in Chrome 157. Because Fenced Frames relied on `FencedFrameConfig` handles from deprecated ad auction and selection APIs, the element can no longer be navigated and serves no functional purpose. Ecosystem consensus favors this cleanup, as removing single-engine experimental surface reduces platform complexity and technical debt.
